To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The reaction of dinitrogen tetroide (N2O4) with polycyclic aromatic hyrdrocarbons (PAHS) and their derivatives is a fast electrophilic reaction.

the reactivity of a PAH in electophilic reactions depends on the structure and the substituents, and that the reactivity can be predicted with the help of spectroscopic constants and theoretical calculations.

the reactivity of polycyclical aromatic hydrocarbons toward nitrating species can be explained by the electron density at the ring, and that the reaction rates are in the same order of magnitude as those of atmospheric reactions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reactivities of PAHS in electrophilically catalyzed atmospheric reactions, in particular with the reaction with nitrogen dioxide and its derivatives.
the chemical reactivity of polycyclical aromatic hydrocarbons in the atmosphere.
the reactivity of polycular aromatic hydrocarbons toward nitrating agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PAH are very reactive toward nitrating species in the environment, and that the reactivities are dependent on chemical structure.
the reactivity of a PAH is determined by its chemical structure and that it is not necessary to know the exact reaction mechanism to be able to predict the reactivity of an unknown PAH.
the reactivity of the PAH is determined by the chemical structure and that the reactivity is higher for those PAH with higher electron density and higher polarizability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the reactivity towards electrophilic nitrating agents of polycyclic hydrocarbons is a function of the number of fused benzene rings, the number and position of the heteroatoms and the substituents, and the presence of functional groups, and that the reactivity can be estimated from the spectroscopic constants.
the reactivities of PA(H) in electrophilical substitution reactions in the atmosphere under dark conditions are related to the chemical structure.
the relative reactivities in the electrophilic substitution of PAH in the atmosphere can be explained by the electron density at the carbon atoms in the PAH.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the reactivity of polycylic aromatic hydrocarbons is not simply related to the number of aromatic rings.
there are many PAHs that are reactive toward electrophilic nitrogen oxides, and the reactivity of the PAHs is related to the electronic structure of the PAH.
PAHs can be oxidized to nitrated PAHs in the atmosphere.
